chunks: "I draw a triangle pointing to the right. The two inputs are on the left side, the flat side, and the output is the point on the right.
I put a minus sign on the upper input and a plus sign on the lower input. The minus is the inverting input and the plus is the non-inverting input.
The names tell you what each one does to the output. If I wiggle the plus input up, the output goes up, same sign. If I wiggle the minus input up, the output goes down.
The output is the gain times plus minus minus, so the two inputs fight each other.
That's also why negative feedback goes back to the minus input: if the output rises, the minus input rises, and that pushes the output back down.
When I'm being careful, I also draw two little supply pins, the positive supply on top and the negative supply or ground on the bottom.
Schematics often leave them out, but the part can't work without them.
And one gotcha: on a schematic people sometimes flip the input order to make the wiring look neater, so I always trust the plus and minus signs, not whether an input is on top."
